- Capture instantly: Highlight a passage anywhere, hit ⌘⇧K, add the source, done.

- Rediscover daily: Today view resurfaces 3–5 saved passages using spaced repetition.

- See the connections: A similarity engine surfaces "This resonates with…" links across everything you've saved.

- Organize your way: Group entries under topic loci, tag them, and track full sources with an Index for your whole collection.

- Add your own voice: Write dated marginalia beneath any passage.

- Read it like a book: Book Mode typesets your collection into a paginated view, exportable to PDF.

- Listen, too: On-device neural narration reads entries aloud with synchronized highlighting, fully private.

- Your files, your way: Stored as plain Markdown, synced free via iCloud or Dropbox — no account, no lock-in.

Start with quotations from eight public-domain classics, or begin blank. Loci is where the passages that shape how you think finally have a home.

apps.name: Alibi
apps.tagline: Book your time before they do
apps.description:
Your calendar is an open invitation. An empty slot reads as "take me".

Alibi fills those slots before anyone else does.

You set two things: how many hours a week you want for yourself, and which days.
Alibi works out the rest. It reads your week and picks the moments where a block
will actually protect something, instead of blindly padding your schedule.

The blocks are real events in Google Calendar. To everyone else you look busy,
because you are. With work.

WHAT IT DOES

Finds room for uninterrupted work in your week and books it.
Declines conflicting invitations, with a message you write yourself.
Moves blocks when the week changes, instead of leaving a stale wall of busy.
Shows how much time you defended, how much was taken, and which days you keep losing.

WHAT IT DOES NOT DO

It never sends invitations or notifications to anyone.
It never touches events it did not create.
It never sends your calendar contents anywhere. Only time ranges are used for
planning: no titles, no descriptions, no names.

HOW YOU USE IT

Two minutes on Monday morning. The rest of the week it sits in the menu bar and
stays quiet.

Requires a Google account. Automatic declining of conflicting invitations works on
Google Workspace accounts. On a personal Gmail account the blocks still hold, just
without auto decline.

The difference: Bench is 100% offline. Every tool runs locally, in-app. Your tokens, payloads, and data never touch a server - no network calls, no accounts, no telemetry. The private alternative to the ad-filled "online dev tools" you've been pasting sensitive data into for years.

Summon it from anywhere with ⌘⇧B, do the thing, and get back to work.

Local. Private. Instant. A tool you'll actually keep in your Dock.

Spin the Wheel turns any decision into a moment of suspense. Add your options, give the wheel a spin, and watch it glide to a winner with smooth, realistic motion — complete with satisfying tick sounds and a confetti celebration when it lands.

Whether you're picking a lunch spot, choosing a raffle winner, assigning chores, or running a classroom game, Spin the Wheel makes every choice feel fair and fun.

apps.name: ForgetMeNot
apps.tagline: Too small to plan, too big to forget
apps.description:
You're deep in a refactor when a Slack ping lands: "can you review my PR later?" It's not worth a calendar block. It's not worth a to-do list ceremony. But if you don't capture it right now, it's gone. 

ForgetMeNot is built for exactly this moment. Hit a shortcut, type a line or grab a screenshot, and a small forget-me-not flower blooms quietly on your screen. That's it. Just a gentle visual breadcrumb sitting at the edge of your attention. Each flower is one loose end. 

ForgetMeNot doesn't try to be your task manager, your second brain, or your productivity system. It's the thing that lives between "I'll remember" and "I need to write this down" — the layer your existing tools have always missed. Stay in flow. Let the flowers hold the rest.

apps.name: Blur: Video Editor
apps.tagline: Blur faces, passwords and private data
apps.description:
Blur is a Mac video editor for hiding sensitive information in video. Blur faces, passwords, API keys, email addresses, phone numbers, names, license plates, bank details and notifications in screen recordings, product demos,
tutorials, Zoom calls and gameplay footage.

Drop in an MP4 or MOV and draw a blur region straight onto the preview — rectangle or ellipse, moved and resized with the mouse, with adjustable blur strength from a light haze to fully unreadable. Add as many regions as you need to censor several things at once.

Everything runs locally on your Mac. No upload, no account, no internet connection. Most ways to blur a video involve sending it to a website, which is an odd thing to do with footage whose whole problem is that it contains something private.

Good for: blurring faces in video, censoring passwords in screen recordings, redacting personal data before sharing a demo, hiding customer names in support recordings, anonymizing footage for GDPR, removing private info from tutorials and bug reports.

apps.name: Helix
apps.tagline: Scientific data analysis, simplified
apps.description:
Helix helps you organize, analyze, and visualize scientific data from raw numbers to publication-ready charts — powered by three trusted open-source engines: Jspreadsheet CE for tables, WebR (R running in WebAssembly) for statistics, and Plotly for graphs. Think of it as a free, minimalist alternative to GraphPad Prism.

Note: this is a foundation in active development. Feedback, bug reports, and feature requests are welcome.

**Data Organization**
- Three-pillar structure — Tables → Analyses / Graphs, with every analysis and graph linked back to its source table
- 4 table types — Column, XY, Grouped, Multiple Variables — each offering the analyses and graphs that fit its data shape
- Spreadsheet-style grid — Copy/paste, undo/redo, multi-cell selection, row/column deletion
- Data exclusion — selectively exclude data points from graphs and statistical analyses

**Statistical Analyses**
Smart guided wizards propose the right test for your table type:
- Column tables — descriptive statistics; compare two groups (Student's t, Welch's t, Mann-Whitney, paired t, Wilcoxon); compare multiple groups (one-way ANOVA, Kruskal-Wallis, repeated-measures ANOVA, Friedman); one-sample t test; identify outliers (ROUT method, Motulsky & Brown, with adjustable false-discovery-rate Q)
- XY tables — correlation, linear regression, nonlinear regression (straight line, sigmoidal 4PL, semilog, hyperbola, polynomials), area under the curve
- Grouped tables — two-way ANOVA, multiple t tests
- Multiple Variables tables — correlation matrix, multiple regression
- Across all tests — post-hoc comparisons (Tukey, Bonferroni, Dunn's) and multiple-comparison corrections (Holm, FDR / Benjamini-Hochberg)

**Graphs**
Each table type offers the chart types that suit its data:
- Column tables — individual values, box & violin plots, mean ± error bars, pie and donut charts
- XY tables — scatter, bar, and area plots; dose-response curves (one-click sigmoidal 4PL with EC50 and Hill slope on the graph); Kaplan-Meier survival curves (censored-subject ticks, from event codes or survivor counts)
- Grouped tables — grouped scatter, bars, lines, stacked bars, horizontal bars
- Multiple Variables tables — heatmaps with selectable color scales (Viridis / Red-Blue / Heat), optional value labels and a legend
Shared across every graph:
- Custom colors — assign a color to each data series, or highlight individual data points; colors are shared by every graph drawn from the same table
- Regression overlay — draw a linked linear-regression fit line, 95% confidence band, and equation with R² directly on scatter plots
- Interactive rendering — zoom in and out, adjust axes thickness and font size
- Resizable graphs — drag any axis to resize, with a live size readout to match dimensions across graphs
- Axis control — manual or automatic min/max/step
- Error bars — SD, SEM, or none
- Significance annotations — stars or p-values with pairwise comparisons
- Export to PNG, JPG, or SVG; copy to clipboard

**Projects & Interface**
- Native `.hlx` project format (JSON-based, fully portable) — open and edit with any text editor
- Native menu bar with keyboard shortcuts
- Decimal separator conversion — automatically convert commas to periods in all spreadsheet numbers (required for R compatibility)
- Light, dark, or automatic theme

apps.name: Hindsight
apps.tagline: Seal your decisions. Meet them later.
apps.description:
Hindsight is a decision journal built around one moment: finding out whether you were right. Write down a decision, what you expect to happen, and how confident you are — then seal it like a letter. On the review date you chose, the letter comes back. Break the seal, compare your prediction with reality, and watch your calibration take shape.

- Seal decisions with a wax-stamp ritual — sealed letters are immutable, no quiet edits after the fact
- Pick a review date, get a quiet reminder when the letter is due, and optionally add review dates to your calendar
- Break the seal to face your past self: record what happened and the one lesson you'd keep
- The Mirror shows your calibration — how often your 80% turned out to be a 50%
- Reviews due at a glance in the menu bar and dock badge
- Export any reviewed decision as a typeset PDF letter, or your whole ledger as Markdown
- Local-first: no account, no cloud, no telemetry

Everything lives on your Mac. The only person Hindsight reports to is the one who wrote the letter.

apps.name: Brez
apps.tagline: Breathing companion for calm focus
apps.description:
Brez is a breathing companion that helps you find calm focus throughout your day.

Long days at the computer add up, back-to-back calls, deep work, little room to breathe. Brez gives you a 30 to 60 second reset, always one click away.

Three breathing techniques, each grounded in science:

• Sigh, the fastest way to release acute stress and tension
• Box, four equal phases to find clarity before a call or a hard task
• Wave, a continuous, effortless breath to let go of accumulated tension

Brez checks in gently a few times a day, and can offer a quick breath before your calendar calls, always quiet during meetings, always easy to dismiss.

Everything happens locally on your Mac. No accounts, no tracking, nothing leaves your device.

One breath at a time.

apps.name: Replenish
apps.tagline: Track household purchases and reorder
apps.description: Replenish is a lightweight desktop app that helps you remember when to rebuy everyday essentials—without managing a full inventory. Log a purchase in seconds (“Purchased Today”), and Replenish automatically tracks how long items last, learns your typical cadence (weekly to yearly), and surfaces what’s due soon with a clear next-buy window. apps.name: Instant MCP
apps.tagline: Your local files, ready for Claude
apps.description:
Instant MCP is the one‑click bridge between the files on your Mac and the Claude Desktop app.

Claude can already work with your local data — but connecting it means editing hidden config files, installing developer tools, and pointing servers at file paths. If that sentence lost you, that's exactly the point. Instant MCP does all of it for you.

Pick a file — a CSV, an Excel sheet, a SQLite database, or a whole folder of CSVs — and Instant MCP connects it to Claude. That's the entire app. No terminal, nothing to install, no JSON to hand‑edit. When it's connected, you see plainly what Claude can now read, with an example question you can copy straight into Claude to try it.

Everything stays on your Mac. Instant MCP never uploads your data, backs up your existing setup before it changes anything, and disconnects just as cleanly as it connects — removing only what it added.

One screen. One decision. The bridge that should have existed all along.

- Visual fretboard shows every note with audio feedback so you learn by ear and sight

apps.name: Noted
apps.tagline: Powerful notetaker just one hotkey away
apps.description:
📝 Toggle open and closed a floating markdown notetaker with just one hotkey. Yes, this is a Raycast Notes alternative, and before you come at me, I’m a huge Raycast fan. There were just some additional features I wanted from Notes so this is my “fork” of it.

It can do most things Raycast Notes does, so let me cover what’s new:

🌟🌟🌟 Highlights 🌟🌟🌟

🔻 Toggle blocks! Stack them with checkboxes, bullet lists, or numbered lists too (see pic 1) 
🦐 When typing, if your cursor gets close to the note’s bottom edge, it'll autoscroll so that you’ll never be typing in a shrimp pose (see pic 2)
💾 Automatic backup and restoration so you never lose your progress again (see pic 4)
🌯 Smart punctuation wrapping: selecting text and pressing ( will wrap the text in ( ) automatically. Fully configurable. (see pic 3)
 ⇅  Move any line up/down, not just list items
❗ A quick animation plays when opening a note to indicate where your cursor is (see pic 1)
👀 Live preview when browsing other notes (see pic 2)

✨✨ Other features ✨✨

➕ Customize the hell out of font size, font color, accent color, background tint, etc
➕ Drag and drop text anywhere
➕ Automatic thousands separator (the commas in 10,000,000). Supports both American and European formats, don’t worry.
➕ Hotkey to toggle floating behavior
➕ Drag and drop notes to reorder or pin/unpin them
➕ Global hotkey to close Noted even when it’s not focused
➕ Export a note as markdown

There are a bunch of other smaller features for you to discover too. Hope you enjoy using the app!

apps.name: Font Finder

apps.description:
Preview fonts in realistic editorial layouts before using them. See how typefaces work together across headlines, subheads, and body copy with editable sample text.

apps.name: Prism
apps.tagline: Work smarter, without leaving your app.
apps.description:
Prism is a native macOS AI command palette that works everywhere you do.

Instead of constantly switching between ChatGPT or any AI assistant and your favourite apps, simply highlight any text, press a keyboard shortcut, and Prism appears instantly beside your cursor. Explain code, rewrite emails, summarise articles, translate documents, fix grammar, brainstorm ideas, or run your own custom AI workflows, all without leaving your current application.

Whether you're writing, coding, studying, researching, or replying to emails, Prism keeps you in flow by bringing AI directly into your existing workflow.

Built for macOS from the ground up, Prism feels like a native system feature rather than another browser tab.

How It Works:
Using Prism takes just a few seconds.
1) Highlight any text
Select text in virtually any macOS application, including:
• Safari
• Mail
• Messages
• Notes
• Slack
• Discord
• VS Code
• Xcode
• Notion
• Obsidian
• Terminal
• And many more.

2) Press your shortcut
Launch Prism instantly with:
⌘⇧Space
A beautiful floating panel appears right beside your cursor, so you never lose your place.

3) Choose an action
Prism includes built-in AI actions like:
• Explain
• Summarise
• Rewrite
• Translate
• Improve Writing
• Fix Grammar
• Generate Reply
• Continue Writing
• Brainstorm
• Ask AI

Or choose one of your own custom actions.

4) Get your result instantly

Review the AI response without leaving your current app.

Then choose to:
• Copy
• Replace the selected text
• Insert below
• Continue the conversation

Everything happens in place, keeping you focused on your work instead of switching between windows.

Custom Actions
Every workflow is different.
That's why Prism lets you create your own reusable AI commands.
Instead of typing the same prompt over and over, save it once and access it with a single click.

Examples include:
Code Review
Review this code for bugs, edge cases, security issues, and performance improvements.
Professional Email
Rewrite this email in a concise and professional tone.
Meeting Summary
Extract key decisions, action items, owners, and deadlines.
Translate Naturally
Translate into fluent French while preserving tone and intent.
Social Post
Rewrite this content into an engaging X post with a strong opening hook.
Once saved, your custom actions are always available whenever Prism appears.
Built for Every Workflow

Whether you're a developer, student, designer, marketer, researcher, or writer, Prism adapts to the way you work.

Developers can explain unfamiliar code, review pull requests, or generate documentation.

Writers can rewrite paragraphs, improve clarity, and brainstorm ideas.

Students can simplify difficult concepts, create study notes, and summarise research papers.

Professionals can draft emails, extract meeting actions, and polish presentations in seconds.

Local First

Your prompts, settings, preferences, and history stay on your Mac.

Use your favourite AI provider—including OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, Ollama, or LM Studio—and choose whether your workflows run in the cloud or entirely on-device.

Prism gives you complete control over your data and your models.

Why Prism?
Because AI should fit into your workflow, not interrupt it.

No browser tabs.

No endless copy and paste.

No breaking your concentration.

Just highlight, transform, and continue working.

It checks in periodically to help you notice distractions, refocus, finish, or save the task for later. Its optional adaptive mode uses local AI to learn which apps support different kinds of work and reduces unnecessary interruptions over time.

apps.name: Relay

apps.description:

Customize the clip length, points per correct answer, and total rounds to match your game style. Track team scores throughout the game and review past matches in your history.

- Configure game rules including clip duration, points, rounds, and playback order

Instant intelligent search — Find files using OCR text, AI-generated descriptions, tags, file names, dates, or natural language searches.

Automatic organization — Capture watches your chosen folders, imports new screenshots, PDFs, and images, then automatically renames and categorizes them.

apps.name: Sole
apps.tagline: One thing, one day — always in view
apps.description:
Sole is a menu bar app for people who lose time to context switching.

Two things live in your menu bar all day: how much of today is left, and what you're working on right now. Everything else — your projects, your backlog, your notes, your history — is one click away in a lightweight dropdown. Nothing forces its way into a separate window you have to manage.
Sole doesn't nag. There are no forced breaks, no pop-up alerts when you go over an estimate, no red "you're behind" warnings. It observes and reflects, quietly, and gets out of your way.

apps.name: Keen Eye
apps.tagline: Track anything. Miss nothing.
apps.description:
Keen Eye lives quietly in your menu bar, watching whatever you tell it to, so you don't have to remember to check.

WATCH ANYTHING
Quick-add crypto prices and wallets, GitHub repo activity, or stocks across 17 global exchanges. Or go further: paste any URL and describe what to track in plain English e.g "the price on this page," "new posts on this blog," "open PR count here" and Keen Eye figures out the rest, powered by Glaze's built-in AI.

NEVER MISS A THRESHOLD
Set alerts the same way you'd text a friend: "notify me when it drops below 60,000." No dropdowns, no config. Voice works too, for free, through macOS's 
built-in dictation.

ONE ICON, EVERYTHING AT A GLANCE
Keen Eye takes up exactly one spot in your menu bar. Pin your most important metric as the hero value so it's visible without a click, or open the popover 
to see everything you're tracking.

Live values, trend arrows, and quick edit/pause/remove in one clean list.

apps.name: GeoLens
apps.tagline: Browse your site as any country sees it
apps.description:
What it does

GeoLens is a one-purpose macOS menu bar tool: view your website the way a visitor from another country would see it, without leaving your desk. You create a "connection" — an identity profile combining country, language, timezone, coordinates, and optionally a proxy carrying a real IP from that country. Hit Launch, and GeoLens opens an isolated Chrome instance (fresh profile every time, no leftover cookies) with spoofed navigator.language, an overridden Intl timezone, spoofed Geolocation API coordinates, and — if enabled — network traffic routed through the target country. From there you just browse normally, click around, and open DevTools if you need to dig deeper.

Real-world use cases

Locale redirects and content: confirm that a German visitor actually lands on /de/, not an English page with a guessed IP-based fallback.
Geo-targeted pricing and currency: many e-commerce sites vary price or currency by network-level location, not browser settings — impossible to verify locally without a real IP from that country.
Geographic restrictions: see for yourself whether content or a service is blocked or altered in a given country, instead of taking it on faith.
hreflang/SEO diffing: the built-in Diff view compares \x3Chtml lang>, canonical tags, titles, and hreflang across several countries at once — catches multi-region markup mistakes fast.
Date/time localization: verify that anything relying on Intl/timezone (schedules, "N hours ago", calendars) computes correctly in another timezone.

Why DataImpulse proxy

Language, timezone, and geolocation are all client-side signals visible to the page's JavaScript. But a site's backend never sees any of that — it only sees your real outgoing IP. If the geo-logic lives server-side (IP-based redirects, IP-based pricing, regional blocks), no amount of browser spoofing will let you test it; you need traffic actually leaving from that country's IP.

DataImpulse is a residential proxy provider. One button, "Generate via DataImpulse," in the connection editor creates proxy credentials that route traffic through an IP in the selected country (219 countries available) — the one piece client-side spoofing can never fake.

Works fully without a proxy, too

Proxy is entirely optional: without it, Chrome simply goes out over the machine's normal internet connection, while language, timezone, and geolocation are still spoofed correctly through an independent mechanism. Proxy only matters when the actual outgoing IP is what's being tested (server-side geo-redirects, IP-based pricing, regional blocks). For anything that depends only on what client-side JS sees — locale content, time calculations, RTL/translations — Country + Language + Timezone alone is enough.

apps.name: Opus
apps.tagline: From idea to sync-ready, on your Mac.
apps.description:
Opus is a music library for producers who are building a real catalog, not just organizing playlists.
Most music tools assume your tracks are already finished and just need uploading somewhere. Opus starts earlier — it tracks your ideas from idea → in progress → sync ready → pitched → licensed, so you always know what's actually ready to send out and what's still just a motif in a folder.

What it does:
- Links your existing audio files (masters, stems, alt mixes) to creative "Tracks," without moving or reorganizing anything on disk
- Tracks versions (full/60s/30s cuts) as a family, not separate unrelated files
- Logs pitches and outcomes per track, so you know who you've already sent something to
- A simple rights/splits record — collaborators, PRO status, license terms — living next to the music itself
- A dashboard that surfaces what needs attention: tracks that are sync-ready but never pitched, pitches that have gone quiet, ideas that have stalled
- One-click export bundles (like a "Sync Pitch Package": full/60s/30s + a one-sheet, zipped and ready to send)

Everything lives locally on your Mac, no subscription, no uploading your masters to someone else's server, no lock-in. It's free, and I built it because I needed it myself.

Why I built this:

I'm a producer building out a sync catalog so the goal is something like 60-80 finished, pitch-ready tracks. The problem was never writing the music. It was everything around it: which version of which idea was actually done, which files I'd already pitched somewhere, which folder had the stems.

I kept starting things and never finishing them, because there was no system telling me what state anything was actually in. So I built one. Opus tracks each idea through its real lifecycle: from a rough motif to something I've pitched to a licensed placement,  and links straight to the actual files on my machine, no uploading, no separate database to keep in sync.

It's not trying to be a marketplace or find you placements. 
It's the boring infrastructure underneath that — the thing that tells you what's actually ready to send out, so you stop guessing. I made it for myself first. If it's useful to you too, that's a bonus.

apps.name: Hanabi

Screen sharing should feel calm before it feels risky. Hanabi is a focused privacy rehearsal where you can practice the moments most likely to expose something private: a sign-in form, a messages workspace, and an unexpected notification.

Compare a synthetic presenter workspace with the viewer preview beside it. Narrow, source-independent matte patches replace tagged demo emails, phone numbers, passwords, API keys, and exact private amounts. Revealing one example is always intentional and confirmed. A surprise-notification exercise visibly holds the last safe preview before showing an already-protected banner.

Everything is synthetic, local, and in memory: no account, upload, external network request, screen-capture permission, OCR, or stored screen content.

Hanabi is a rehearsal and protected-preview demonstrator. It does not alter an existing Zoom, Meet, Teams, or system screen share and does not claim to protect arbitrary live pixels.

apps.name: Golden Hour
apps.tagline: The light where you are, all day long
apps.description:
Golden Hour isn't a weather app or a sun-times tracker. It's an ambient window — a quiet, living sky you leave open on your Mac that shifts with the real light where you are.

Through the day, the whole window is the sky. It moves from deep-indigo night through blue hour into the warm mauve-and-amber of golden hour and back again, computed from the real sun for your city. The sun rides low and blooms warm as it sets into the ridge; at night a pale moon takes over, stars come out, fireflies drift along the hills, and a few windows glow in the dark.

It tells you what you actually want to know — how long the good light will last — in one quiet line, without a single chart or dashboard. Golden hour and blue hour are the moments it's built around: the light you'd step outside for.

Drag the timeline to move through the whole day and watch everything respond. Turn on Desktop Mode to let the sky fill your screen as a calm, living backdrop behind your work. Flip on the gentle soundscape and the room fills with the ambience of the hour. Change your city and it all recomputes — offline, always.

Each mark lands on a hidden canvas, colored by whichever app/domain is in front. Xcode days lean one way, Figma days another. At midnight the painting is finished and filed away, and tomorrow starts blank.

It doubles as a time tracker. You can see how long you were actually working, your longest unbroken stretch, how often you jumped between apps, and where the hours went, app by app and site by site. Those numbers live on your Mac and nowhere else.

Features:

- Live canvas: watch today's painting grow in real time as you work

- Daily gallery: each day becomes one finished artwork, rendered in high resolution at midnight and kept forever

- Time tracking: active time, longest focus stretch, app switches, and where the hours went by app and site

- Three art styles: Liquid Metal (dark chrome), Flow Silk (glowing threads), and Liquid Glass (pooled droplets), with more on the way

- Wallpaper: set any painting as your desktop, or let it refresh automatically each day

- Focus radio: a small built-in player with a few lofi and ambient stations

- Private by design: no permissions to grant, no account, and none of your data ever leaves your Mac

On how the tracking works: nothing is recorded except timing. Verdigris never sees which keys you press, what you read, or what's on screen. Just when you were active and which app was in front, plus the site's domain if you opt in.

apps.tagline: The app that refuses to write for you

Every writing tool is racing to write for you. Nib is the one that believes writing = thinking.

Nib lives in your menu bar and listens only to the writing you hand it. Draft or paste in its pad, or capture anything you've written with a keystroke. When a habit repeats like hedging, jargon, burying the ask, Nib shows you one observation. 

--
Just three lines:
1. Your sentence. 
2. The principle. 
3. And how a master handled it.

Your hedge next to Lincoln's wartime telegram. Your "circle back" next to Fowler's plain-words rule from 1906. Your buried request next to five words that ended a war: "Let the thing be pressed.”

--
The gap between your words and the master's is the lesson. That's the point. Writing is thinking, and no one can do your thinking for you.
One observation a day, at most. Nib earns your attention by almost never asking for it.

For people who still write — and want to get better at it.

apps.name: Insomniac
apps.tagline: Smart Keep-Awake Utility for Developers
apps.description:
Ever lost your live debug state because your Mac decided it was time for a nap?

Insomniac is a lightweight, native macOS menu bar utility built specifically for developers who need their screens to stay awake while coding, compiling, and debugging. No more jiggling the mouse or digging through System Settings—Insomniac handles your power state intelligently in the background so you can stay in the flow.
Key Features

•	Smart App Detection: Insomniac watches your workflow. Add your essential tools (like Glaze, Cursor, or Claude) to the Watchlist, and Insomniac will automatically lock your screen awake the second they become active. When you switch away, normal sleep rules immediately resume.

•	Set It & Forget It: Toggle "Launch at Login" to have Insomniac run silently in your menu bar from the moment you boot up, ready to catch your active debug sessions without any manual input.

•	Precision Timers: Need to force a heavy build process without auto-detection? Use the Pomodoro-style manual timer. Set your duration, and Insomniac will run a native caffeinate -d process until the countdown ring hits zero.

•	Late-Night Aesthetics: Customize your menu bar and center ring with Dark Mode optimized icons. Choose from the signature glowing Acid Pill, the classic Coffee Mug, the Energy Drink, or the Debugging ladybug to match your setup.

•	Zero Bloat: Built natively in Glaze, Insomniac directly hooks into the macOS terminal to manage power states securely and efficiently, without draining your battery or hogging system resources.

Stay focused, keep your display alive, and never let a screensaver ruin your debug session again.

apps.name: Bloop
apps.tagline: Blogging with a Human in the Loop
apps.description:
Fully automated AI blogging almost always produces the same thing: generic, soulless content that reads like a thousand other articles. Bloop takes a different approach. It uses AI to do the heavy lifting - research, structuring, drafting - while keeping a human firmly in control at every single step. The result is content that's fast to produce, but never feels machine-made: sharp, unique, and genuinely optimised for how people and AI search engines discover content today.

Bloop guides you through a structured editorial journey - from your very first scattered ideas, through a fully researched outline, to a publish-ready article - with the AI proposing and you deciding at every checkpoint. Nothing gets locked in without your approval, and you can always go back, edit, and regenerate from any point without losing your progress.

Key Features:

• A guided, multi-stage writing workflow: capture raw ideas, feed in research, build a gap-checked outline, generate content section by section, and finalise metadata, all in one continuous editorial flow with full editing control at every stage.
• Built-in competitive research: pull in competitor blog URLs and YouTube video transcripts directly into your project, so the AI drafts with real context instead of guesswork.
• Human-editable AI outlines - review, rewrite, reorder, or add headings and subheadings before a single word of final content is generated, keeping structure entirely in your hands.
• Section-by-section content generation: expand and refine ideas heading by heading, review and edit each section as it's written, and build the article progressively instead of getting one uneditable AI dump.
• SEO, GEO & AEO-aware writing engine: built-in optimisation for search engines and generative AI answer engines: semantic keyword coverage, question-style headings, entity consistency, and structured content designed to get cited, not just ranked.
• Multi-brand project management: save reusable brand profiles (tone of voice, author bio, terminology glossary, defaults) and apply them instantly to any new project across multiple websites or blogs.
• Flexible AI engine support: use your Glaze AI credits, or connect your own OpenRouter API key to write with the model of your choice.
• A closing quality checklist: a built-in, persistent checklist for final publishing steps like images, alt text, and internal linking, so nothing gets missed before you hit publish on your website.

Bloop doesn't try to replace the writer. It replaces the blank page and the tedious, repetitive parts of research and structuring while making sure the final voice, judgment, and quality control stay exactly where they belong: with you.

apps.name: Commonplace
apps.tagline: A commonplace book for digital libraries
apps.description:
John Locke kept a commonplace book for twenty-five years before publishing, in 1685, the method he'd developed to make it usable: an indexing system for retrieving any passage by topic without re-reading the whole notebook. That was manual labor then.

Commonplace automates it now. Your clippings are already scattered—years of Kindle highlights, Kobo annotations, or Logos clippings, each locked inside its own platform and undiscoverable. Commonplace imports all of it and tags every clipping by topic automatically, so an insight you underlined five years ago is still usable today.

Import & Review 
Commonplace imports directly from the PDF exports generated by Kindle, Kobo, and Logos—with step-by-step instructions for retrieving each export from its source app. Before anything is added to your library, review every extracted clipping and swipe to keep or reject it, so your commonplace book stays exactly as curated as you want it.

Automatic Topic Tagging 
Every clipping is analyzed and tagged by topic automatically, using your choice of Glaze AI or a local Ollama model. Correct or refine tags anytime, and merge overlapping topics into one.

Browse 
- See every book in a cover grid, with covers extracted directly from your imports. You may also upload your own covers.
- Sort your library by title, author, or most recently added.
- Browse clippings by topic, or filter clippings within a single book or a single author by topic.
- Browse every author across your entire library

Find Anything, Instantly 
Search your entire commonplace book by keyword, topic tag, author, or book title.

Share & Export 
Share any clipping through the macOS share sheet, or export clippings from a book, author, or topic—tags intact—as a CSV file.

Rediscover
Your homepage shuffles through your entire commonplace book, weighted toward the clippings you haven't revisited in the longest time—so nothing you've ever kept quietly collects dust. It's the difference between a filing cabinet and a living conversation with what you've already read.

Your Stats
A dedicated stats page gives you the full picture: total clippings, books, and topics, clippings added this year, your most-clipped book, your most-clipped topic, your most-clipped author, and a visual record of your clipping activity over time.

aiCapability.purpose: Suggests topical tags for your highlighted passages so you can browse your commonplace book by topic.

apps.name: Dock Shifter
apps.tagline: Flip your Dock. Save your neck.
apps.description:
Dock Shifter lets you instantly move your macOS Dock from left to right, or anywhere, with a single click or on a fully automated weekly schedule. Designed for multi-monitor users and anyone who needs to change their screen layout daily.

⚡ What You Can Do
One-Click Flip
Hit the Flip button at the top of the app, and your Dock instantly swaps between left and right. The button always shows you where it's headed next.

Manual Positioning
Prefer full control? Use the Left / Bottom / Right segmented control to place your Dock exactly where you want it, any time you want.

Weekly Auto-Schedule
Enable the weekly schedule and assign a Dock position — or "No change" — to each day of the week. Dock Shifter will automatically apply the right position once per day, so your setup is always ready before you even sit down. Today's day is clearly marked in the schedule so you always know where you stand.

💡 Why I Built This
My monitor setup changes every day, literally. Depending on the day, my main screen sits on my left or my right, which means my Dock is always on the wrong side and my neck is always paying the price. My physician flagged it: constantly looking in the same direction was causing real, repetitive strain. I looked for a solution, found nothing simple enough, and built Dock Shifter.

apps.name: Radical
apps.tagline: The visual calendar; time, reimagined.
apps.description:
Your year as a landscape, your day as a circle.

Traditional calendars are good at showing your next event, but not how your time fits together. Yearly / monthly views can often lose context or become too crowded, and the level of information given doesn’t match the view. 

Radical is a visual calendar, where you can see your time in new ways, ooo! Step back to understand your whole year and bigger plans, then zoom into a circular 24-hour view to focus on today.  

- See the year at a glance: spot busy periods, open stretches and bigger plans in one continuous view. Show or hide the details depending on what you want to see.

- See the shape of your day: events on a 24-hour clock can help visual thinkers and fellow neurodivergent folks like me! 

- Create events by typing naturally: type “tomorrow at 2pm” or “next Friday”.

Findle is a keyboard-first palette for moving and copying files, without ever opening a second Finder window.

1. Select your files in Finder.
2. Hit your hotkey. A floating palette appears with your selection ready to go.
3. Type a few letters to fuzzy-search any folder in your home directory. Results are ranked by match quality and how often you actually use that folder.
4. Press Enter to move, or ⌘-Enter to copy. No drag, no drop.

Need to go deeper? Arrow right to enter a folder and search inside it, arrow left to back out. A breadcrumb keeps you oriented, and moving or copying a file is always one keystroke away.

Every operation gets a toast with an instant Undo, plus a global undo hotkey that works from anywhere. Name conflicts never overwrite silently. You choose Keep Both, Replace, or Skip, right in the palette.

Findle lives in your menu bar. Trigger the palette, check your last destination, or undo a recent move straight from the tray. All three hotkeys are remappable, and if a shortcut is already taken, Findle rolls back automatically instead of breaking.

It's built with native macOS surfaces and vibrancy, follows your system accent color, and shows real Finder icons everywhere.

Key Features:

- Global hotkey summons a Spotlight-style palette, no extra Finder window
- Fuzzy search across your home folder, ranked by relevance and recency
- Drill-down navigation with breadcrumbs
- Move (Enter) or Copy (⌘-Enter) in one keystroke
- Toast + Undo after every operation, plus a global undo hotkey

apps.name: Meanwhile
apps.tagline: Did you mean to be doing this?
apps.description:
⌘ An app that asks, at random moments, whether you meant to be doing this.

Write down how you mean to spend this time. One line, in your own words. Later, at a moment you can't predict, a card shows you your own words back and asks whether you meant this. You answer yes or not really, and it disappears.

Drifting is quiet. You rarely notice the moment you left, which is why a scheduled reminder doesn't catch it: you learn its rhythm, you brace for it, you stop seeing it. Meanwhile never arrives at the same time twice. It cannot be anticipated, so it can't become part of the background.

The method comes from psychology. In experience sampling, people are paged at random moments and asked what they're doing. Killingsworth and Gilbert used it to show we spend close to half our waking hours thinking about something other than what we're doing.

It's not a timer and not a task list. Nothing is blocked, nothing is timed, nothing is scored. It never asks whether you got anything done, only whether you meant this.

There's also a mode with no card at all: just the chime. For when what you mean to return to is already in your head.

Over time it leaves you a record of the distance between what you meant and what happened. You can read it yourself, or export it and let an AI tell you what it sees.

It lives in the menu bar. What you write stays on your Mac.

apps.name: Thooval
apps.tagline: Write. Publish. Own.
apps.description:
## The Blog Editor Andrej Karpathy Wished Existed

A desktop Markdown editor that helps you write, generate, and publish directly to GitHub Pages.

Your words. Your files. Your blog. No platform required.

Distraction-free blogging, from an idea to a local Markdown file to a live website.

## The Idea

In January 2024, Andrej Karpathy tweeted about his ideal blogging platform: write in Markdown with a complete WYSIWYG editor, deploy to clean static pages, add analytics and comments, and truly own your files forever.

He explored everything, including Medium, Substack, Jekyll, and Typora, before concluding:

> “I don’t believe this exists.”

**Thooval is that thing.**

## Turn an Idea Into a Full Blog Post

Not sure how to begin?

Give Thooval a prompt, topic, or rough idea, and its AI-powered writing assistant can generate a complete blog post for you.

Use the result as a first draft, reshape it in the editor, or keep only the parts that help. You remain in control of every word.

The generated post is saved as a regular Markdown file in your local folder, just like anything you write yourself.

No proprietary format. No locked content. No separate publishing workflow.

**Start with a prompt. Finish with a post you own.**

## Write Without Distractions

Thooval is a desktop app with a beautiful, distraction-free WYSIWYG editor for writing in Markdown.

There are no split views and no raw syntax. You simply write.

Create a post from scratch or generate a full first draft with AI. Then edit, rewrite, expand, and refine it directly in the same focused editor.

Add images by dragging them into the editor, pasting them, or selecting them from your computer. Everything is saved automatically to a local folder on your machine.

Your posts remain plain Markdown files that you can open in any editor, move anywhere, and keep forever.

There is no vendor lock-in, and you do not need an account just to write.

## Publish in One Click

When you are ready to share your work, click **Publish**.

Thooval generates a clean, minimal static website with no bloat and no JavaScript frameworks. Just fast, simple HTML.

It then publishes the site to GitHub Pages, giving your blog a real public URL within seconds.

You can also add Google Analytics or Plausible for traffic insights, enable Giscus for comments, and connect a custom domain.

That is it.

**Generate ideas. Write locally. Publish globally. Own everything.**

## What Thooval Includes

### ✨ AI-Powered Generation

Turn a prompt, topic, or rough idea into a complete blog post.

Generate a first draft in seconds, then edit it freely until it sounds like you.

The final post is stored locally as plain Markdown and remains completely under your control.

### ✍️ Writing

A complete WYSIWYG Markdown editor that lets you focus entirely on your words.

Write from scratch, refine an AI-generated draft, and add images by copying and pasting, dragging and dropping, or selecting them from your computer.

### 🚀 Publishing

Thooval renders your writing as simple, minimal static HTML and hosts it on GitHub Pages at a clean URL.

Publishing takes one click.

### 📊 Maintaining

Built-in support for Google Analytics, Plausible Analytics, and Giscus comments.

Everything is available from one place, without the usual setup complexity.

### 🔓 Ownership

Your posts are Markdown files stored in a folder on your computer.

Whether you write every word yourself or begin with an AI-generated draft, you have complete access, complete export control, and permanent ownership.

Move your writing anywhere, at any time.

apps.name: Enough

apps.description:
Most productivity apps help you do more. Enough helps you stop.

Each morning, Enough asks one question: what would make today enough? You name up to three things, protect one block of deep work, and when you finish, a real singing bowl rings and the app tells you to stop.

Anything still on your mind goes into a sealed jar the app will not open until tomorrow. Unfinished tasks pull at your attention long after you leave the desk, and writing them down somewhere trusted is what releases the pull. The seal makes the trust real: you cannot peek, so your evening is actually yours. The list dies at midnight.

Then you sew the day closed. Sashiko is the Japanese practice of mending fabric with visible stitches, one small repeated gesture that turns repair into meditation, and the mend into something more beautiful than the original cloth. Enough borrows both ideas. The closing ritual ends with one slow, hand-drawn stitch, and every day, closed or unfinished, gets sewn into a year-long pattern generated from your days. No streaks and no gaps, because a uniform life would make the dullest fabric. The variation is the pattern. In December you print it.

⚡ 3 Core Modes
✏️ Draw Mode — Doodles to Parallel Assets: Draw a rough sketch anywhere on screen to instantly generate 5 parallel output nodes (3D Object, Vector Icon, Clean Diagram, SVG Illustration, and UI Wireframe). Pick your favorite and drop it straight into Figma.

Refine with Text: Prompt your sketch to instantly tweak materials, lighting, or style (e.g., "convert to frosted glass") across all 5 generated asset variations without redrawing.

🎯 Redline Mode — Direct Layer Editing: Redline or sketch directly over live UI or 3D elements on your screen. Describe your change, and Skeche generates matching vector elements dropped straight into your Figma layer tree.

📖 Read Mode — Specs to Architecture: Circle any text spec, documentation, or PRD on your screen. Skeche reads the semantic context and instantly converts raw text into structured system diagrams or SVG illustrations.

🚀 How to Use (3 Quick Steps)
Summon Over Any App: Press ⌘⌥D (Cmd + Option + D) anywhere on your OS—over Figma, your browser, or your IDE—to activate Skeche in standard windowed mode without switching full-screen spaces.

Sketch, Circle, or Redline: Draw a rough idea, redline directly over an existing UI component, or circle raw text/PRD specs on your screen.

Refine & Drop: Use text prompts to tweak styles or materials in real time, then drag your favorite generated node directly into your open Figma layer tree or copy the raw SVG code.

🛠️ Key Highlights
Ambient OS Utility: Runs smoothly in normal screen mode over any active workspace via ⌘⌥D (Cmd + Option + D), respecting native OS space hierarchies.

Figma-Native: Drops generated vectors directly into your open layer hierarchy.

Fallback History Panel: Automatically saves every generated node, prompt, and sketch locally so you can restore past variations or pick up previous iterations without losing your flow.

Instant Export: Drag assets directly into your workspace, copy raw SVG code, or export PNGs.

apps.name: Arrival
apps.tagline: Connected drives into workflows.
apps.description:
Arrival is a native macOS menu-bar utility that turns removable storage devices into automatic workflows.

Register a voice recorder, camera card, USB drive, external SSD, or other removable device, then tell Arrival what should happen whenever it connects. Arrival can recognize the device, find the files you want, copy them to a selected folder, verify the transfer, launch another application, and let you know when the job is complete.

Arrival is designed for photographers, videographers, audio professionals, attorneys, consultants, field researchers, and anyone who regularly moves files from removable storage into a repeatable workflow.

For example, you can configure Arrival to detect a voice recorder, find its new audio files, copy and verify them, organize them into a dated folder, and then launch your transcription application. A photographer can assign a different workflow to a camera card that imports selected media files and opens the destination in Lightroom, Capture One, Photo Mechanic, or another application.

Features in Arrival 1.0
Native macOS menu-bar app
Runs in the background while its main window is closed
Detects connected removable drives and memory cards
Register and name individual devices
Writes a secure Arrival identity tag to configured devices
Recognizes known devices when they reconnect
Create reusable workflows and assign them to multiple devices
Browse and select a specific source folder on a connected device
Filter files by extension and include subfolders when needed
Import all matching files, the newest files, or files not previously processed
Copy files using a safe temporary-file process
Verify transfers with SHA-256 hashing
Track processed files to prevent repeat imports
Choose how duplicate files are handled
Create dated destination folders
Use basic folder and filename templates
Show live transfer progress
Cancel an active transfer
Reveal the destination in Finder
Launch a selected application after import
Open imported files with another application
Optionally eject the device when finished
Native macOS notifications
Distinct status sounds
Optional spoken completion and error announcements
Activity history for completed, cancelled, and failed workflows
Automatic recovery awareness for interrupted transfers
Launch at login
Quiet hours and privacy controls
Built for safe file handling

Arrival does not mark a transfer complete simply because a copy was started. Files are copied to a temporary destination, verified, and then moved into their final location only after the transfer succeeds.

If a source device is disconnected, a destination becomes unavailable, or verification fails, Arrival reports the problem without presenting an incomplete file as a successful import.

Arrival also keeps executable workflow settings on the Mac rather than trusting instructions stored on removable media.

A practical first release

Arrival 1.0 is the first public release of an actively developed application. The core workflow is functional and has already been used to import and verify real files from removable storage, including an 81-file voice-recording import followed by launching an external transcription application.

This release focuses on the essential workflow:

Connect a device → recognize it → find new files → copy and verify them → launch the next step → report the result.

Additional workflow actions, templates, interface improvements, notification options, and automation features will continue to be developed.

Arrival is local-first and does not require a cloud account to recognize devices, copy files, verify transfers, or maintain its activity history.

Created by Rich Washburn
richwashburn.com

3. Video Tools: Compress videos, convert formats, trim clips, extract audio, create GIFs, optimize files for sharing, and more.

PDF Toolkit is designed for the people who work with documents every day:
1. Students submitting assignments, lecture notes, resumes, and project reports.
2. College graduates preparing job applications, portfolios, certificates, and important documents.
3. Professionals and corporate employees handling contracts, invoices, presentations, reports, HR documents, and client files.

Whether you're preparing a last-minute assignment, applying for your dream job, or managing documents at work, PDF Toolkit eliminates repetitive file-management tasks with a clean, intuitive interface that feels right at home on macOS.

apps.name: ClockScreen
apps.tagline: Your Mac's display, reimagined your way
apps.description:
Beautiful, highly customizable clock displays for your Mac desktop that can surface useful real-time info right when you need it. Finally, a free app where you can have personal, aesthetic screensavers to showcase anywhere! Please read the story below if you’d like more info. Look at the latest release notes for the app to see if there are any small issues that have not been fixed yet. If there are not any issues in the release notes, that means the app is stable!

Key Features:
- Design custom clock screensavers with multiple style options, fonts, and layouts, with support for digital and analog displays
- Create groups to sort all of your clocks into
- Make your clock super personal to you by displaying a custom photo, your favourite colours, or any upcoming events, to always make it a joy to look at!
- Choose from no motion to fast motion on all moving clock backgrounds—all of them are designed to be very efficient on battery
- Choose between designing a clock display or a widget display, or generate your own AI clock background, as well as add your own unique photo
- Add real-time info to your clocks, like weather in your area, your current Mac battery, your next calendar event or reminder, and any upcoming birthday from your contacts
- Over 30 other ways to customize how your clock looks to make it truly personal to you

The Story: I got this idea because I wanted an app on my Mac just to display a nice clock whenever I walked into my room. However, all the apps I tried either didn’t have the features I wanted, or all of them were locked behind a paywall. When Raycast announced Glaze in Private Beta and I got access about a month later, I knew I had to build this. So I got to work, building a highly customizable clock app that you can use as your daily screensaver. And now, I can share it with the world. In v8.0.0, ClockScreen has gotten even more useful, surfacing real-time info right when you need it on a clock that matches your personal aesthetic. This update makes the app so much more personal to you, with the ability to create your own backgrounds. So now I’m here, excited to share my app with the world! It might be simple—not life-changing or anything—but I think it has some real potential due to how customizable it is, making it so simple to glance at your display and see everything you need for the day. This app could also be useful for teachers, as they could put a simple clock up using a widget display, with, for example, custom text to let them know how much time they have left on an assignment. I really hope people like it. I will keep improving this app in the future with updates, and I will always listen to user feedback.

One thing I love about this app is that it’s polished to the very last pixel, with very few inconsistencies. I designed it this way to make the app a joy to use, getting to what you need right away, and I really hope people notice this work. This makes the app so seamless to use every day, with a clean UI to guide you everywhere. This app is great for people who want to, for example, display a clock on their monitor or TV so they can see real-time info anytime during the day to know what’s coming next.

If you need an introduction to the app, you can find a video showcasing its features on my X profile. I have also posted this in the #show-and-tell channel in the Glaze Slack Community! Hope you enjoy the app!

apps.name: Saulamandra
apps.tagline: The assistant for the freelance lawyer
apps.description:
Before Saulamandra, there was Saul.

Before he was Saul Goodman, he was Jimmy McGill: one lawyer, no staff, no IT department, and a law office in the storage room at the back of a Vietnamese nail salon. His archive was the boot of a yellow Suzuki Esteem with a mismatched door. His diary was his memory. His accounting was a pile of 700 dollar public defender cheques he had to argue about. And the case that changed his life, Sandpiper, began as a bin bag of shredded documents he and his brother taped back together strip by strip, by lantern light, on a kitchen table  logo.

Here is the uncomfortable part: Jimmy was good. He found the case nobody else found, he built it, he proved it. What he did not have was structure. No reliable way to compute a deadline, no record of the hours he burned, no single place where a matter lived from the first phone call to the final invoice. Every solo practice knows that feeling. The talent is there. The scaffolding is not.

And then there was Chuck, the brother who would not allow a single powered device inside his house. Played for drama on screen, but strip away the illness and you are left with an instinct any lawyer recognises: some information should not leave the room logo. Professional privilege is not a setting you tick in a cloud dashboard. It is the whole job.
Salamandra is the tool Jimmy never had, built on the discipline Chuck never stopped demanding. Case files with a real lifecycle instead of a shoebox. A deadline engine that computes working days under Spanish procedural rules and refuses to accept the result until a human has verified it twice. Hours that get logged the moment they happen, and turn into invoice lines without anyone rebuilding a spreadsheet at midnight. All of it local, encrypted, on your machine, leaving only when you decide it leaves.

The name is not an accident either. The salamander was the creature that walked through fire without burning, and running a small practice is mostly fire. Deadlines, clients, invoices, all at once, all on you.

So yes, there is a bit of Saul in Saulamandra. Just the good half. S'all organised, man.

apps.name: Mina — Terminal Companion
apps.tagline: Explains commands before you run them
apps.description:
You found a command on the web or an AI wrote one for you. Now what?

Paste it into Mina. Before anything runs, you get a plain-language explanation of what the command does, what it changes, and whether that change can be undone. Nothing executes until you say so.

That explanation is not an LLM guess. Mina's analysis is deterministic and runs entirely on your Mac: no network call, no model, nothing about your command leaves the machine. It parses the shell structure and matches against 679 built-in command definitions, and when it doesn't recognize a program, Mina says so instead of calling it safe. 

Placeholders like \x3CAPI_KEY> and YOUR_USERNAME become labeled fields you TAB through. A value used four times is one editable field. Quoting and escaping are handled for you, including inside quoted strings, so you stop hunting through a wall of text to edit one argument.

Mina is built for the moment your AI agent has to stop. When Claude, Codex, or a local agent hits a password, a login, an approval it cannot grant, or something it simply cannot do, it can hand the command to Mina through the bundled CLI. You type the secret locally. It never enters the model's context, and Mina's transport keeps it out of the process arguments where ps could read it. Mina also knows what your agent's flags mean: it recognizes the ones that turn the guardrails off, like --dangerously-skip-permissions, --yolo, and --sandbox danger-full-access, and makes you acknowledge them explicitly.

Beginners get a Terminal that explains itself. Everyone else gets a review layer for the commands worth reading twice.

Scritch is a scratchpad that lives in your menu bar. Press one hotkey and it appears — over any app, even fullscreen ones — ready before your thought has time to escape. Press Escape and it's gone. No windows to find, no documents to name, no save button anywhere.

It's for the wifi password. The half-formed idea. The thing someone said in a meeting that you'll need in an hour. The code snippet that doesn't belong anywhere yet. Notes too small and too fast for a "real" notes app — which somehow end up being the notes that matter most.

SCRIBBLE IT DOWN
One global hotkey, from anywhere on your Mac. The window appears instantly and your cursor is already in the right place — the exact note, scroll position, and cursor position you left. Pin the window to keep it floating above your work, or let it slip away the moment you click elsewhere.

WRITE IN MARKDOWN
Type the syntax, see it styled — headings, bold, lists, quotes, and dividers render live as you write. Dashes become bullets. Brackets become checkboxes you can actually click. Underneath it all, your notes are plain markdown: copy anything out of Scritch and you get clean, portable text. No lock-in, no proprietary format, no ceremony.

PASTE YOUR CODE
Fenced code blocks and inline snippets are styled properly, right in the middle of a thought. Scratch notes and scratch code belong in the same place.

FIND IT AGAIN
Unlimited notes, a fuzzy quick switcher, and full search across everything you've written. Type a few characters and jump. If the note doesn't exist yet, create it from the same keystroke.

MAKE IT YOURS
Themes with light and dark variants. Your choice of font, text size, line height, and line width. Show the Dock icon or hide it. Show the word count or don't. Launch at login so Scritch is simply always there.

QUIET BY DESIGN
Everything autosaves continuously. Local daily backups happen on their own. Your notes are stored on your Mac and can be exported as plain markdown files at any time. No account, no subscription to think about, nothing between you and the text.

Scritch does one thing: it catches what you're about to forget, faster than anything else on your Mac.

Pick your paper: yellow legal pad, white lined, grid, or dotted. Choose your ink from seven colors, and give each page its own handwriting style — five fonts, from a casual scrawl to a tidy print to a typed look. apps.name: Telltale
apps.tagline: See your Mac's state. Don't read it.
apps.description:
Telltale tells you when your Mac's condition changes. Heat, memory pressure, network, CPU load — each becomes a brief full-desktop effect — and when a process is behind it, that process is named in the menu bar and logged so you can ask later. The rest of the time it draws nothing at all.

**60-second walkthrough:** https://youtu.be/4mAsfkCw8Nk

Sailors tape a short length of yarn to the sail: wind is invisible, the yarn isn't. It's called a **telltale**. Your Mac hasn't got one — it's throttling, it's swapping, something you forgot about is pulling 40 Mbps, and the standard answer is a menu bar of graphs four pixels tall.

- **Heat rises** — flame licks up from the bottom edge, and holds while it's critical
- **Memory tightens** — a dark fluid rises; cross into swap and hairline cracks spread through it
- **Something starts pulling bandwidth** — rain falls, tinted per app
- **Load spikes** — heat shimmer along the edges

Each fires on the *change*, then fades. Steady state draws nothing, because a signal that's always on tells you nothing. **Recent events** keeps the last 200 crossings — what happened, what caused it, how long it held — so "why was my Mac slow twenty minutes ago?" has an answer, with a colour legend above it so the per-app tints are decodable.

Presets for **Subtle** (default), **Full** continuous tracking, or **Alarm only** — every effect selectable, and a master kill switch.

A monitor that degrades the machine it watches is a joke about itself, so Telltale holds **under 3% of one CPU core** by default — shedding frame rate, particles, then whole effects as it nears that ceiling, thermal fire last. Locked, idle, or on battery it stops — the battery pause and the throttling are both yours to switch off.

No Accessibility. No Screen Recording. No TCC prompt, ever — everything it draws comes from your Mac's own vitals, and the event log is a local file of process names as macOS reports them, which never leaves your Mac. The overlay is click-through everywhere and stays out of full-screen apps.

Any app or script can trigger an effect:

```
open "telltale://effect/fire?stage=critical&duration=5&label=Deploy%20failed"
```

Wire it to a finished build, a failing deploy, a long agent run. The label sits in the menu bar for the length of the event and goes into the log with it, so you can tell the flames you asked for from the ones you didn't. Settings → About lists every form of the URL — click one to see it fire, or copy it as a runnable command.

Or write your own: start from one of six worked examples, describe one and Glaze AI writes the shader, or paste GLSL from your own agent — same live signals, same governor, same URL triggers, shed first because it's your code and not mine.

apps.name: PlainType
apps.tagline: Formatting in, plain text out
apps.description:
Paste text the way you meant it: plain. PlainType strips formatting, hidden characters, and stray markup from whatever you copy, so what lands is clean text and nothing else.

Copying from Notion, Slack, a PDF, or an AI chat drags along more than you can see. Bold markers, smart quotes, non-breaking spaces, zero-width characters, and wiki-link syntax follow the text into your code editor, your terminal, your CMS, and your forms, where they break search, mangle diffs, and fail validation for no visible reason. PlainType removes all of it.

How it works:
Turn on auto-clean and every copy is stripped the moment it hits your clipboard. Prefer control? Leave it off and clean on demand with a global shortcut. Either way, your original stays untouched until you paste.

What it removes:
Bold, italic, and heading markup. Smart quotes, curly apostrophes, and fancy dashes. Non-breaking and zero-width spaces. Wiki-links, list markers, and stray tabs. Collapsed blank lines and trailing whitespace.

Built to stay out of your way:
Runs quietly in the menu bar. A recent history shows exactly what was cleaned and lets you re-copy any result. Everything happens on your Mac. Nothing you copy ever leaves your device.

PlainType. Plain text, every time you paste.
